description: Evidence-based systematic phonics (structured literacy) for ages ~4-8, family co-learning with parent coach insights; older learners can use the same steps at a faster pace. Learners, not students.

lessons.title: Hearing Sounds in Words
lessons.topic: Words are made of small sounds. Before reading letters, we train our ears: what sound do you hear at the start of 'sun'? At the end of 'dog'?
lessons.example: Mom says 'mmmop.' Leo, 4, says the first sound is 'mmm'.
lessons.activity: Play I Spy with sounds: 'I spy something that starts with /b/.' Then try ending sounds. 10 minutes in the car or kitchen.
check_questions: Say the very first sound in your own name.
Pick something in the room and tell its last sound.
Do 'cat' and 'cup' start the same or differently? Explain how you know.
lessons.steelman: FOR: Systematic, explicit phonics is supported by a large body of research (e.g. the US National Reading Panel, 2000) as an effective way to teach most children to read. AGAINST: Some children pick up sounds naturally through rich reading aloud; too many drills can feel like a chore, so keep it playful.
lessons.kid_explanation: Words are made of small sounds. Before reading letters, we train our ears: what sound do you hear at the start of 'sun'? At the end of 'dog'?
lessons.parent_coach_insight: This is phonemic awareness: hearing sounds without letters. Say sounds, not letter names ('mmm', not 'em'). Stretch words slowly. Correct gently: point to the tricky letter and ask 'what sound does this make?' rather than saying 'wrong.' Decode first; do not encourage guessing from pictures or the first letter. Keep practice short and daily (10-15 minutes). If after steady practice a learner still struggles a lot to link letters and sounds, reverses many letters well past age 7, or reading is far behind peers, it can help to talk with a reading specialist or pediatrician; early support works well and says nothing bad about the learner. Older learners who missed phonics can use the same steps at a faster pace with grown-up examples.

lessons.title: Short Vowels & Blending CVC Words
lessons.topic: Letters stand for sounds. Short vowels: a (apple), e (egg), i (itch), o (octopus), u (up). Blend sounds together: s-a-t makes sat, p-i-n makes pin.
lessons.example: Ava, 5, taps s-a-t and sweeps her finger: 'sat!'
lessons.activity: Make paper letter tiles (index cards cut up). Build 3-letter words, swap one letter (sat→sit→pit) and read each.
check_questions: Build a word with your tiles and read it to a grown-up.
Change one letter in your word to make a new word. What did it become?
Which vowel sound was hardest today, and why?
lessons.steelman: FOR: Systematic, explicit phonics is supported by a large body of research (e.g. the US National Reading Panel, 2000) as an effective way to teach most children to read. AGAINST: Vowel sounds vary by accent and some children need much more practice; going too fast can frustrate.
lessons.kid_explanation: Letters stand for sounds. Short vowels: a (apple), e (egg), i (itch), o (octopus), u (up). Blend sounds together: s-a-t makes sat, p-i-n makes pin.
lessons.parent_coach_insight: Teach a few consonants plus one short vowel at a time. Use continuous sounds (s, m, f) first because they are easier to blend. Finger-tap each sound, then sweep to blend. Correct gently: point to the tricky letter and ask 'what sound does this make?' rather than saying 'wrong.' Decode first; do not encourage guessing from pictures or the first letter. Keep practice short and daily (10-15 minutes). If after steady practice a learner still struggles a lot to link letters and sounds, reverses many letters well past age 7, or reading is far behind peers, it can help to talk with a reading specialist or pediatrician; early support works well and says nothing bad about the learner. Older learners who missed phonics can use the same steps at a faster pace with grown-up examples.

lessons.title: Segmenting & Spelling with Sound Boxes
lessons.topic: Spelling is blending backwards: say a word, break it into sounds, write a letter for each sound. Sound boxes help: one box per sound.
lessons.example: Max, 6, pushes three buttons for m-a-p, then writes map.
lessons.activity: Dictation game: say 5 CVC words; learner uses sound boxes and writes them. Check together, letter by letter.
check_questions: Say a word of your own and push a coin for each sound.
How many boxes did your word need? Show a grown-up.
What is one word you spelled today that you feel proud of?
lessons.steelman: FOR: Systematic, explicit phonics is supported by a large body of research (e.g. the US National Reading Panel, 2000) as an effective way to teach most children to read. AGAINST: Spelling develops more slowly than reading; invented spelling early on is normal and some argue it should be allowed freely.
lessons.kid_explanation: Spelling is blending backwards: say a word, break it into sounds, write a letter for each sound. Sound boxes help: one box per sound.
lessons.parent_coach_insight: Draw 3 boxes; learner pushes a coin into a box for each sound, then writes letters. Praise correct sounds even if a letter is off. Correct gently: point to the tricky letter and ask 'what sound does this make?' rather than saying 'wrong.' Decode first; do not encourage guessing from pictures or the first letter. Keep practice short and daily (10-15 minutes). If after steady practice a learner still struggles a lot to link letters and sounds, reverses many letters well past age 7, or reading is far behind peers, it can help to talk with a reading specialist or pediatrician; early support works well and says nothing bad about the learner. Older learners who missed phonics can use the same steps at a faster pace with grown-up examples.

lessons.title: Digraphs: sh, ch, th, ck
lessons.topic: Sometimes two letters work together to make one sound: sh (ship), ch (chip), th (thin), ck (duck).
lessons.example: Mia, 6, spots 'sh' in shop and reads it as one sound.
lessons.activity: Digraph hunt: find sh, ch, th, ck in a picture book or cereal box. Write each find on a card and read the stack.
check_questions: Find a digraph somewhere in your home and read the word.
How many sound boxes would 'ship' need? Show why.
Make up a silly sentence using two of the digraph teams.
lessons.steelman: FOR: Systematic, explicit phonics is supported by a large body of research (e.g. the US National Reading Panel, 2000) as an effective way to teach most children to read. AGAINST: English has exceptions (ch in 'school'); learners may feel confused, so explain that patterns help most of the time, not always.
lessons.kid_explanation: Sometimes two letters work together to make one sound: sh (ship), ch (chip), th (thin), ck (duck).
lessons.parent_coach_insight: In sound boxes a digraph goes in ONE box. Teach ck comes after a short vowel at the end of short words. Correct gently: point to the tricky letter and ask 'what sound does this make?' rather than saying 'wrong.' Decode first; do not encourage guessing from pictures or the first letter. Keep practice short and daily (10-15 minutes). If after steady practice a learner still struggles a lot to link letters and sounds, reverses many letters well past age 7, or reading is far behind peers, it can help to talk with a reading specialist or pediatrician; early support works well and says nothing bad about the learner. Older learners who missed phonics can use the same steps at a faster pace with grown-up examples.

lessons.title: Blends: st, bl, fr
lessons.topic: Blends are two consonants side by side where you still hear both sounds: st (stop), bl (black), fr (frog).
lessons.example: Leo, 6, reads 'lap' then 'flap', hearing the new f.
lessons.activity: Sand tracing: pour sand or salt on a tray, trace blend words with a finger while saying each sound aloud.
check_questions: Say a word that starts with a blend and tap each sound.
How is a blend different from a digraph? Use your own example.
Add a sound to the start of a word you know to make a new word.
lessons.steelman: FOR: Systematic, explicit phonics is supported by a large body of research (e.g. the US National Reading Panel, 2000) as an effective way to teach most children to read. AGAINST: Some children hear blends as one sound and need patient ear training; others find this step quick.
lessons.kid_explanation: Blends are two consonants side by side where you still hear both sounds: st (stop), bl (black), fr (frog).
lessons.parent_coach_insight: Unlike digraphs, each blend letter gets its own sound box. Practice adding one sound at a time: top→stop. Correct gently: point to the tricky letter and ask 'what sound does this make?' rather than saying 'wrong.' Decode first; do not encourage guessing from pictures or the first letter. Keep practice short and daily (10-15 minutes). If after steady practice a learner still struggles a lot to link letters and sounds, reverses many letters well past age 7, or reading is far behind peers, it can help to talk with a reading specialist or pediatrician; early support works well and says nothing bad about the learner. Older learners who missed phonics can use the same steps at a faster pace with grown-up examples.

lessons.title: Long Vowels: Silent e
lessons.topic: A silent e at the end can make the vowel say its name: cap→cape, kit→kite, hop→hope.
lessons.example: Ava, 7, adds an e card to 'cub' and reads 'cube'.
lessons.activity: Make an 'e' card. Build short words with tiles, add the e card, and read both versions.
check_questions: Pick a word you can change by adding e and read both.
What happens to the vowel when the e is added? Say it your way.
Find a word in a book that follows this pattern.
lessons.steelman: FOR: Systematic, explicit phonics is supported by a large body of research (e.g. the US National Reading Panel, 2000) as an effective way to teach most children to read. AGAINST: Exceptions exist (have, give, love); some teachers prefer teaching these alongside so learners are not surprised.
lessons.kid_explanation: A silent e at the end can make the vowel say its name: cap→cape, kit→kite, hop→hope.
lessons.parent_coach_insight: Show the pair side by side; the e is silent but changes the vowel. Use 'jumping e' language if it helps. Correct gently: point to the tricky letter and ask 'what sound does this make?' rather than saying 'wrong.' Decode first; do not encourage guessing from pictures or the first letter. Keep practice short and daily (10-15 minutes). If after steady practice a learner still struggles a lot to link letters and sounds, reverses many letters well past age 7, or reading is far behind peers, it can help to talk with a reading specialist or pediatrician; early support works well and says nothing bad about the learner. Older learners who missed phonics can use the same steps at a faster pace with grown-up examples.

lessons.title: Vowel Teams: ai, ee, oa
lessons.topic: Some vowel teams work together for one long sound: ai (rain), ee (feet), oa (boat).
lessons.example: Max, 7, finds 'ee' in tree and green.
lessons.activity: Vowel team sort: write words on paper slips and sort them into ai, ee and oa piles. Read each pile aloud.
check_questions: Read a word with a vowel team you found today.
Sort three words into the right team piles. Explain one choice.
Write one word with a vowel team without looking.
lessons.steelman: FOR: Systematic, explicit phonics is supported by a large body of research (e.g. the US National Reading Panel, 2000) as an effective way to teach most children to read. AGAINST: English has many vowel spellings; some argue learners should also rely on context and wide reading, not only patterns.
lessons.kid_explanation: Some vowel teams work together for one long sound: ai (rain), ee (feet), oa (boat).
lessons.parent_coach_insight: Teach one team at a time with lots of reading. Mention common alternates (ay at word end: day) only after the main pattern is secure. Correct gently: point to the tricky letter and ask 'what sound does this make?' rather than saying 'wrong.' Decode first; do not encourage guessing from pictures or the first letter. Keep practice short and daily (10-15 minutes). If after steady practice a learner still struggles a lot to link letters and sounds, reverses many letters well past age 7, or reading is far behind peers, it can help to talk with a reading specialist or pediatrician; early support works well and says nothing bad about the learner. Older learners who missed phonics can use the same steps at a faster pace with grown-up examples.

lessons.title: Heart Words (High-Frequency Words)
lessons.topic: Some common words have a tricky part you learn 'by heart': the, said, was, of. Decode the regular parts, then put a heart over the tricky part.
lessons.example: Mia, 7, draws a heart over the 'ai' in 'said'.
lessons.activity: Heart word cards: write 5 words, draw a heart over the tricky part, and play a quick find-and-read game daily for a week.
check_questions: Read a heart word and show where its tricky part is.
Which part of that word follows the normal sound rules?
Use one heart word in a sentence of your own.
lessons.steelman: FOR: Systematic, explicit phonics is supported by a large body of research (e.g. the US National Reading Panel, 2000) as an effective way to teach most children to read. AGAINST: Some programs teach sight words by memorizing whole shapes; research favors connecting letters and sounds, but practice and repetition still matter.
lessons.kid_explanation: Some common words have a tricky part you learn 'by heart': the, said, was, of. Decode the regular parts, then put a heart over the tricky part.
lessons.parent_coach_insight: Don't treat these as whole-shape memorization. Show which letters follow the rules and which don't; that sticks better. Correct gently: point to the tricky letter and ask 'what sound does this make?' rather than saying 'wrong.' Decode first; do not encourage guessing from pictures or the first letter. Keep practice short and daily (10-15 minutes). If after steady practice a learner still struggles a lot to link letters and sounds, reverses many letters well past age 7, or reading is far behind peers, it can help to talk with a reading specialist or pediatrician; early support works well and says nothing bad about the learner. Older learners who missed phonics can use the same steps at a faster pace with grown-up examples.

lessons.title: Fluency & Understanding
lessons.topic: Reading well means reading the words smoothly and understanding them. Read a short story, then tell it back: who was in it, what happened, and why.
lessons.example: Leo, 7, rereads a short story three times and retells it to his grandma.
lessons.activity: Family story time: learner reads a decodable book aloud twice, then retells it using fingers: who, what, why.
check_questions: Retell a story you read in your own words.
Who was the main character, and how do you know?
Why do you think something in the story happened?
lessons.steelman: FOR: Systematic, explicit phonics is supported by a large body of research (e.g. the US National Reading Panel, 2000) as an effective way to teach most children to read. AGAINST: Understanding also depends on vocabulary and background knowledge, so reading aloud rich books to learners remains important alongside decodables.
lessons.kid_explanation: Reading well means reading the words smoothly and understanding them. Read a short story, then tell it back: who was in it, what happened, and why.
lessons.parent_coach_insight: Use decodable stories that match the patterns learned. Reread the same text a few times for smoothness. Ask who/what/why after, without quizzing harshly. Correct gently: point to the tricky letter and ask 'what sound does this make?' rather than saying 'wrong.' Decode first; do not encourage guessing from pictures or the first letter. Keep practice short and daily (10-15 minutes). If after steady practice a learner still struggles a lot to link letters and sounds, reverses many letters well past age 7, or reading is far behind peers, it can help to talk with a reading specialist or pediatrician; early support works well and says nothing bad about the learner. Older learners who missed phonics can use the same steps at a faster pace with grown-up examples.

lessons.title: Writing Sentences
lessons.topic: A sentence starts with a capital letter, has spaces between words, and ends with a mark (. ? !). Write about your day!
lessons.example: Ava, 7, writes 'I fed my dog.' with a capital, spaces and a period.
lessons.activity: Daily journal: each learner writes 1-3 sentences about their day; a parent writes one too. Read them to each other at dinner.
check_questions: Write a sentence about your day and read it aloud.
Check your sentence: what goes at the start and at the end?
What could you add to make your sentence more interesting?
lessons.steelman: FOR: Systematic, explicit phonics is supported by a large body of research (e.g. the US National Reading Panel, 2000) as an effective way to teach most children to read. Explicit sentence-writing practice supports both spelling and composition. AGAINST: Forcing perfect spelling early can discourage writing; some favor free writing first and corrections later.
lessons.kid_explanation: A sentence starts with a capital letter, has spaces between words, and ends with a mark (. ? !). Write about your day!
lessons.parent_coach_insight: Use sound boxes for unknown words; accept phonetic spelling of untaught patterns, gently fix taught ones. Say the sentence aloud first, count the words, then write. Correct gently: point to the tricky letter and ask 'what sound does this make?' rather than saying 'wrong.' Decode first; do not encourage guessing from pictures or the first letter. Keep practice short and daily (10-15 minutes). If after steady practice a learner still struggles a lot to link letters and sounds, reverses many letters well past age 7, or reading is far behind peers, it can help to talk with a reading specialist or pediatrician; early support works well and says nothing bad about the learner. Older learners who missed phonics can use the same steps at a faster pace with grown-up examples.
